# S5 Variants of the conversion

## Example profiles in main Figure 1

The two examples are selected deterministically from the retained radiosondes, rather than chosen for a large improvement. For each sounding, we use the observed level closest to 2 km within 1.7--2.3 km above its surface. We define a temperate (Köppen C) summer-day class (June--August and 07--19 h local solar time) and a continental (Köppen D) winter-night class (December--February and outside 07--19 h); southern-hemisphere seasons are shifted by six months. Within each class we select the sounding whose vector of three surface-referenced conversion errors is closest in Euclidean distance to the three class medians. Station identifiers, dates, class counts, individual errors and class medians are retained in `paper_fig1_soundings.csv` with the analysis outputs. The summer example also shows that the virtual-temperature/GPT3 conversion does not improve every individual sounding. Its profile approximates virtual temperature, while the radiosonde profile shows measured air temperature; humidity aloft is not reconstructed.

## Humidity, lapse rate and height convention

The corrected conversion uses ERA5 2 m air temperature $T$, 2 m dewpoint $T_d$ and surface pressure $p_0$. With $T_d$ in degrees Celsius and pressure in Pa, vapour pressure is $e=611.2\exp[17.67T_d/(T_d+243.5)]$ [@bolton1980], specific humidity is $q=0.622e/(p_0-0.378e)$, and the reference virtual temperature is $T_v=T(1+0.608q)$ with $T$ in kelvin. These are computed quantities. Pairing 2 m temperature/dewpoint with surface pressure approximates a common near-surface reference; the 2 m vertical separation is not corrected explicitly. The subsequent linear profile uses the GPT3 temperature lapse rate as an approximation to the lapse rate of virtual temperature. We do not retrieve humidity aloft or integrate an observed-time humidity profile.

The GPT3 lapse rate is $L(d)=a_0+a_1\cos(2\pi d/365.25)+b_1\sin(2\pi d/365.25)+a_2\cos(4\pi d/365.25)+b_2\sin(4\pi d/365.25)$ [@landskron2018]. All five grid coefficients are used, in K m$^{-1}$ after conversion from K km$^{-1}$. The implementation evaluates the integer UTC calendar day $d$ (1 January is day 1), without fractional days or a southern-hemisphere date shift. It interpolates spatially between 1° grid centres, with longitude wrap; beyond the outer latitude centres it holds the edge latitude while interpolating in longitude. The TU Wien reference routine retains fractional days and uses a single nearest cell in the polar cap; the evaluated R implementation therefore is not identical in these details. Neither implementation linearly interpolates between dates. Values with $|L|<10^{-5}$ K m$^{-1}$ are replaced by $-10^{-5}$ K m$^{-1}$ in the evaluated conversion. This numerical safeguard is separate from the −9.5 to −2 K km$^{-1}$ bounds used below for a fitted season--latitude variant.

The equations use constant standard gravity, $g=9.80665$ m s$^{-2}$. ERA5 surface geopotential is divided by this value; IGRA supplies geopotential heights. No separate geometric-height correction is applied. Under the spherical approximation $z=R_EH/(R_E-H)$, where $H$ is geopotential height and $R_E=6371$ km, geometric height exceeds $H$ by approximately 0.6 m at 2 km and 5.7 m at 6 km above sea level. These values describe the height convention, not an additional error estimate measured in our data. Ground barometer heights and terrain datasets have their own surveyed/geoid references, so our use of a common altitude label does not establish metre-level equivalence of every vertical datum.

## Fitted temperature-profile variants

We tested variants of the column temperature on the radiosondes, with 20 random 50/50 station splits for those with fitted parameters (fitting on one half, evaluating on the other; @tbl-cv). Fitted lapse rates minimise the bird-weighted squared error. The lapse rate varying with season and latitude, $L = b_1 + b_2 a + (b_3 + b_4 a)\cos(2\pi(d - 15)/365.25)$, with $a$ the absolute latitude divided by 90° and $d$ the day of year (southern hemisphere shifted by six months), has $b$ = (`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", lvp$value), collapse = ", ")`) K/km and is kept between −9.5 and −2 K/km; the upper bound only applies poleward of ~`r round(fcl$lat_bind)`° in mid-winter, for `r pct(fcl$share_clamped)` of the bird-weighted levels, and removing it changes the MAE by `r sprintf("%.2f", fcl$mae - fcl$mae_wide)` m. GPT3 needs no fit; on its 1° grid it matches the fitted lapse rates over the heights birds fly and does better above 1 km (@fig-formula).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cv
#| tbl-cap: "In-flight error of the height above the ground over the heights birds fly (bird-weighted, m), mean over 20 held-out station halves. GPT3 variants are not fitted and are evaluated on the same halves."
kab(fcv[, .(Variant = method, Bias = r1(bias_mean), MAE = r1(mae_mean), RMSE = r1(rmse_mean))])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-formula
#| fig-cap: "Bias (a) and SD (b) against height for the standard conversion and the variants with fitted lapse rates."
rfig("formula_height")
```
